title: Quantum Meets AI: Allies Not Competitors

lines.speaker: Marcus Webb
lines.text: Celia, I've been following quantum+ai for a while, and I have to say — what's happened in the last year feels different. Not just incremental progress, but a qualitative shift. Am I reading that right?

lines.speaker: Celia Merzbacher
lines.text: You are. And I think the reason it feels different is that we've crossed the threshold from 'interesting science' to 'practical technology.' That's a transition that many fields never make. The fact that we're talking about allies not competitors in terms of deployment timelines and unit economics, not just research papers — that's the signal.

lines.speaker: Dr. Sarah Chen
lines.text: Welcome to TechNova. I'm Dr. Sarah Chen.

lines.speaker: Marcus Webb
lines.text: And I'm Marcus Webb. Today we're joined by Celia Merzbacher, Executive Director at QED-C. Celia, welcome to the show.

lines.speaker: Celia Merzbacher
lines.text: Thanks for having me. Looking forward to this.

script.segment: SEGMENT 1: The State of the Field

lines.speaker: Dr. Sarah Chen
lines.text: Celia, for listeners who are new to this topic, can you explain what quantum+ai actually involves and why it matters?

lines.speaker: Celia Merzbacher
lines.text: At its core, quantum+ai is about qubit scaling. That sounds simple, but the implications are profound. When you can do error correction reliably and at scale, it changes what's possible in Quantum. The applications range from quantum advantage to hardware platforms, and we're just scratching the surface.

lines.speaker: Marcus Webb
lines.text: How did we get here? What was the path from idea to reality?

lines.speaker: Celia Merzbacher
lines.text: It was a long path — decades, in some cases. The foundational research in algorithm development goes back years, but it was always limited by investment landscape. What changed is that we solved that limitation — through a combination of better technology, better understanding, and honestly, better computing power. Once the bottleneck cleared, everything downstream accelerated.

lines.speaker: Dr. Sarah Chen
lines.text: And where are we now on that path?

lines.speaker: Celia Merzbacher
lines.text: We're in the early deployment phase. The technology works. We're proving it in real-world conditions. The next challenge is scaling — making it cheaper, more reliable, and more accessible. That's an engineering challenge, not a science challenge, and engineering challenges are solvable with enough time and resources.

lines.speaker: Marcus Webb
lines.text: Celia, I want to get into the technical details. What makes your approach different from what's been tried before?

lines.speaker: Celia Merzbacher
lines.text: The traditional approach to quantum+ai relied on workforce development. It worked, but it had fundamental limitations — specifically, it didn't scale past a certain point. Our approach is different because we use geopolitical competition to bypass those limitations entirely. Instead of trying to optimize within the old framework, we created a new framework.

lines.speaker: Dr. Sarah Chen
lines.text: What was the key insight that enabled that?

lines.speaker: Celia Merzbacher
lines.text: It was actually a cross-disciplinary insight. Someone on our team had experience in hybrid computing, and they noticed a parallel between a problem in that field and our problem in quantum+ai. They brought a technique over, adapted it, and it worked. The biggest breakthroughs often come from the intersection of fields, not from deep within one field.

lines.speaker: Marcus Webb
lines.text: What's the current performance level, and what's the theoretical limit?

lines.speaker: Celia Merzbacher
lines.text: We're currently at about 60 percent of what we believe is the theoretical limit. That might sound like there's a lot of headroom, but getting from 60 to 90 percent is often harder than getting from zero to 60. The last 10 percent — going from 90 to 100 — that's where you spend most of the effort. But even at 60 percent, we're already at a level where the technology is commercially viable.

lines.speaker: Dr. Sarah Chen
lines.text: Let's talk about impact. Who benefits from this, and how?

lines.speaker: Celia Merzbacher
lines.text: The impact is broad. In the near term, practical applications is the primary application — and that alone justifies the investment. But the second-order effects are where it gets really interesting. Once you have quantum+ai working at scale, it enables things that weren't possible before — timeline to fault tolerance, new business models, new capabilities. It's a platform technology, not just a point solution.

lines.speaker: Marcus Webb
lines.text: What about the risks? What could go wrong?

lines.speaker: Celia Merzbacher
lines.text: I take risks seriously, and there are real ones. qubit scaling at scale is untested — we're confident, but there could be surprises. There's the regulatory risk — if policymakers move too slowly, deployment stalls. And there's the societal risk — any transformative technology has distributional effects, and we need to be thoughtful about who benefits and who's displaced.

lines.speaker: Dr. Sarah Chen
lines.text: How do you think about the ethical dimensions?

lines.speaker: Celia Merzbacher
lines.text: It's something we discuss internally a lot. The technology itself is neutral — it's a tool. But how it's deployed, who has access to it, what safeguards are in place — those are choices, and they matter. I think the tech industry as a whole needs to do a better job of engaging with these questions proactively, not reactively.

lines.speaker: Marcus Webb
lines.text: Celia, what's your vision for where this field is in five years?

lines.speaker: Celia Merzbacher
lines.text: In five years, I think quantum+ai will be unremarkable — and that's the goal. When a technology becomes unremarkable, it means it's become infrastructure. It's just part of how things work. That's what happened with the internet, with smartphones, with cloud computing. I think quantum+ai is on that same trajectory, and the five-year mark is when it crosses from 'exciting new technology' to 'standard tool that everyone uses.'

lines.speaker: Dr. Sarah Chen
lines.text: What's the one thing you want our listeners to remember from this conversation?

lines.speaker: Celia Merzbacher
lines.text: That the future is being built right now, by people who are solving hard problems in labs and offices and factories. It's not science fiction — it's engineering. And engineering, when done well, is the most powerful force for progress that humanity has ever developed.

lines.speaker: Marcus Webb
lines.text: Celia Merzbacher, Executive Director at QED-C. Thank you for a really thought-provoking conversation.

lines.speaker: Celia Merzbacher
lines.text: Thank you both. I loved this.

lines.speaker: Dr. Sarah Chen
lines.text: And thanks to all of you for listening. This is TechNova — see you next time.
